findings.title: Unbounded recursion decoding nested field-tables/arrays: ~5 wire bytes buy one stack frame
findings.impact: Any peer that can publish a message the victim consumes can kill the consumer's connection thread with a StackOverflowError, repeatably. A nested table costs 5 bytes per level on the wire ('F' plus a 4-byte length), so about 50 KB of header data - comfortably inside a default 128 KB frame - yields roughly 10,000 recursive frames. StackOverflowError is an Error, not an IOException: it unwinds straight past the MalformedFrameException handling this decoder relies on, so the failure lands wherever the reader loop happens to catch Throwable, if anywhere. No MITM, no hostile broker and no TLS downgrade is needed - an honest broker forwards the header table intact, so the attacker only needs write access to an exchange the victim reads from.
findings.evidence: readFieldValue case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable, whose loop calls readFieldValue (line 150); case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray, whose loop calls readFieldValue (line 245). There is no depth argument, counter or nesting limit anywhere in the file - the only bound on nesting is the size of the JVM thread stack.
findings.recommendation: Thread an int depth through readFieldValue/readTable/readArray, increment it on the 'F' and 'A' cases, and throw MalformedFrameException past a small cap (AMQP 0-9-1 has no legitimate use for more than a few levels). Enforce it inside readFieldValue itself, not only at the public entry points, since readFieldValue is package-visible and is also driven by ContentHeaderPropertyReader.

findings.title: readBytes allocates an attacker-chosen array of up to 2 GiB before reading a single content byte
findings.impact: Nine bytes on the wire ('S' or 'x' plus a 4-byte length, or a bare long-string method argument) make the client allocate up to ~2 GiB. readFully then throws EOFException because the bytes were never there, but the allocation has already happened: OutOfMemoryError or a multi-second stop-the-world pause, in a JVM that is usually shared with unrelated application work. This is reachable before authentication - readLongstr backs Connection.Start's server-properties, mechanisms and locales and Connection.Secure's challenge - so a hostile endpoint, a hijacked route, or any MITM on a plaintext AMQP connection triggers it without credentials.
findings.evidence: final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()); if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE) { final byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength]; in.readFully(buffer); - the length is taken verbatim from the peer and the array is sized from it before any content is read. The single guard admits everything up to 2147483646; it exists to avoid an int overflow, not to bound memory. Nothing compares contentLength with the bytes actually remaining in the frame.
findings.recommendation: Refuse to allocate more than what is actually available: check contentLength against in.available() (the same assumption the readTable/readArray loops already make) and/or against the negotiated frame max or a configurable maximum body size, throwing MalformedFrameException otherwise. If very long strings must be supported later, read incrementally into a growing buffer capped at the negotiated limit rather than sizing an array from a hostile integer.

findings.title: Declared table/array lengths are never validated against the bytes remaining in the frame
findings.impact: An over-declared table length makes the decoder run past the end of the table and swallow the bytes that follow it - the remainder of the content-header property list, or the remaining method arguments - re-interpreting them as table entries. The result is not a rejected frame but a silently wrong parse: properties the peer really did send (delivery-mode, expiration, user-id, correlation-id) come back absent or wrong, and the Java client and the broker end up disagreeing about the meaning of the same bytes. Under-declaring truncates the table just as quietly, because the loop stops on available() rather than on a byte count.
findings.evidence: readTable: long tableLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()); ... new DataInputStream(new TruncatedInputStream(in, tableLength)); while(tableIn.available() > 0). Identical pattern in readArray at lines 240-244. unsignedExtend admits values up to 4294967295 and neither length is ever compared with the enclosing frame's remaining payload.
findings.recommendation: Validate tableLength/length against the remaining input (in.available(), or the declared frame payload size threaded down from the frame reader) and raise MalformedFrameException on a mismatch. Drive the loops off a consumed-byte counter against the declared length so that a table which does not end exactly on its boundary is an error rather than a short map.

findings.title: No cap on the number of decoded table entries or array elements: 20-40x memory amplification
findings.impact: Every field the peer packs into a table or array becomes a boxed object plus a HashMap entry or ArrayList slot. One-byte fields ('V' costs a single byte, 'b' and 't' two) therefore expand by roughly 20-40x in heap terms, and those objects stay live for as long as the application holds the delivered message's headers - far longer than the frame buffer. There is no entry-count limit to fall back on, so the cost scales with whatever frame size was negotiated. Cheap, sustained heap pressure from a peer that is otherwise behaving.
findings.evidence: readArray: while(arrayIn.available() > 0) { Object value = readFieldValue(arrayIn); array.add(value); } with an unbounded ArrayList; readTable's loop at line 148 is the same shape with a HashMap. Every primitive case in readFieldValue (in.readByte(), in.readBoolean(), in.readUnsignedShort(), ...) autoboxes.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a maximum entry count per table and per array, and a maximum total number of decoded values per frame, rejecting anything beyond it with MalformedFrameException. Combine with the length validation in F-003 so the bound is checked before the objects are built, not after.

findings.title: Duplicate table field names are accepted and silently resolved first-wins
findings.impact: A table carrying the same field name twice is not rejected; the client keeps the first occurrence and discards the second without a word. Anything else on the path that resolves duplicates the other way, or that routes on the raw bytes - a headers exchange, a broker plugin, a proxy, a shovel, an application written against another client library - reads a different value for the same header out of the same message. Where a header carries something security-relevant (tenant id, signature, an authorization or routing tag that application code checks) that is a header-smuggling primitive: one message on the wire, two readings, and the party doing the enforcement is not necessarily the party the Java consumer agrees with.
findings.evidence: if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value); - the first binding wins and the later one is dropped, with no error and no log. AMQP 0-9-1 requires field names within a table to be unique, so the duplicate is a malformed table being repaired rather than reported.
findings.recommendation: Reject a repeated field name with MalformedFrameException. If compatibility forbids that, pick the policy explicitly, document it, make the encoder agree with it, and log the collision - silently discarding a field the peer sent is the worst of the three options.

findings.title: An empty headers table returns an immutable map while a non-empty one returns a mutable HashMap
findings.impact: The mutability of the map an application receives depends on remote input. The extremely common pattern of reading a delivery's headers and adding to them before re-publishing or forwarding works for every message that carries at least one header and throws UnsupportedOperationException on the first message whose headers table is empty - a remotely triggerable crash in consumer code, on a branch most test suites never produce.
findings.evidence: if (tableLength == 0) return Collections.emptyMap(); whereas the normal path at line 145 returns new HashMap<String, Object>(). The two return types differ in contract, chosen by a wire value.
findings.recommendation: Return an empty HashMap on the zero-length path so the contract does not depend on the peer, or make both paths return an unmodifiable map and say so in the javadoc of readTable() and of the header accessors.

findings.title: Timestamp decoding multiplies a peer-controlled 64-bit value by 1000 with silent overflow
findings.impact: The seconds value comes straight off the wire and the multiplication wraps for magnitudes above ~9.2e15, so a peer can steer the resulting Date to essentially any instant it likes - including one far in the past or future - and the decoder reports no error. Application logic that trusts the AMQP timestamp for expiry, ordering, dedup windows or audit records can be pushed around by whoever published the message, and an out-of-range value is indistinguishable from a legitimate one.
findings.evidence: return new Date(in.readLong()*1000); - a plain long multiply on unvalidated input, no range check and no overflow check.
findings.recommendation: Use Math.multiplyExact and convert the ArithmeticException into MalformedFrameException, or range-check the seconds value against what Date can represent before scaling.

findings.title: Field names are decoded with lenient UTF-8, so invalid byte sequences collapse to the same key
findings.impact: Malformed UTF-8 is accepted and turned into U+FFFD rather than rejected, so byte sequences the peer and the broker treat as distinct field names arrive at the application as one and the same String. Composed with the first-wins duplicate policy in F-005 this becomes a usable pair: send two fields whose raw names differ, watch them collapse into one key on the Java side, and the client keeps whichever arrived first while other components on the path keep both.
findings.evidence: return new String(b, "utf-8"); - the replacing String constructor, which substitutes U+FFFD for every malformed sequence rather than signalling. No CharsetDecoder with CodingErrorAction.REPORT anywhere in the read path.
findings.recommendation: Decode with a CharsetDecoder configured onMalformedInput/onUnmappableCharacter(CodingErrorAction.REPORT) and translate the CharacterCodingException into MalformedFrameException; also prefer StandardCharsets.UTF_8 over the charset-name overload.

findings.title: Build and test dependencies pinned to branches that no longer get security maintenance
findings.impact: Nothing here reaches library consumers - all four are test or build scope - so the exposure is to whoever runs the build: the generate-sources step executes groovy-all 2.4 and the integration-test profile stands up a Jetty 9.4 server on the build machine. Fixes published on the currently maintained branches of these projects will never reach this build, and the gap only widens.
findings.evidence: jetty.version 9.4.58.v20250814 (line 70), groovy.all.version 2.4.21 (line 81, last release of the 2.4 line), logback.version 1.2.13 (line 64) and slf4j.version 1.7.36 (line 58, terminal release of the 1.7 line) - all end-of-life branches, while the shipped compile-scope dependencies are kept current.
findings.recommendation: Move the test and build dependencies onto supported branches (Jetty 12, Groovy 4, Logback 1.5, SLF4J 2.x) as a build-infrastructure task; treat it as hygiene for CI hosts rather than a consumer-facing exposure, and keep it clearly separated from the shipped dependency set.
